item.title: The Bestselling Books of the Week, According to All the Lists
item.dc:creator: Community
item.description: USA Today, Publishers Weekly, NYT, Amazon, and Indie Booksellers all have their own bestseller lists. Here are the combined results.
item.content:encoded:
This week’s bestselling books roundup has three titles appearing here for the first time. Unsurprisingly, one is Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty, the sequel to Big Little Lies, set ten years after the events of the first book. We also have the newest from a bestselling Australian thriller author, Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth.

Last and least is Going Further: The Incomparable Clarence Thomas by Ted Cruz. This seems like a good time to mention that Anita Hill, who spoke at the 1991 Clarence Thomas Supreme Court hearings about the sexual harassment she faced, has her own book: Believing: Our Thirty-Year Journey to End Gender Violence. We simply don’t have the space to get into why it’s disappointing to see a book by Ted Cruz about Clarence Thomas on the bestseller list, but suffice to say, neither of them reflects the ethos of Book Riot.

This list continues to lack diversity on many levels, including being disproportionately by white authors. Some Indie Bestsellers you should know about are Cool Machine by Colson Whitehead, Taiwan Travelogue by Shuang-zi Yang and translated by Lin King, and The Serviceberry by Robin Wall Kimmerer.

To get these numbers, we look at The New York Times, both Combined Print & E-Book Fiction and Combined Print & E-Book Nonfiction lists; Amazon Charts, both Fiction and Nonfiction; Publishers Weekly; USA Today; and Indie Bestsellers, Fiction and Nonfiction, both Paperback and Hardcover.

Books On All Five Bestseller Lists:

Theo of Golden by Allen Levi

Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke

Dungeon Crawler Carl by Matt Dinniman

Whistler by Ann Patchett

The Calamity Club by Kathryn Stockett

Books On Four Bestseller Lists:

Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty (Publishers Weekly, USA Today, NYT, Indie Bestsellers)

Books On Three Bestseller Lists:

Brain Damage by Freida McFadden (Publishers Weekly, USA Today, NYT)

Going Further: The Incomparable Clarence Thomas by Ted Cruz (Publishers Weekly, NYT, Amazon)

Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan (NYT, Amazon, Indie Bestsellers)

Strangers by Belle Burden (NYT, Amazon, Indie Bestsellers)

Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth (NYT, Amazon, Indie Bestsellers)

Find more news and stories of interest from the book world in Breaking in Books.

item.title: 10 Bi4Bi Romance Novels
item.dc:creator: Julia Rittenberg
item.description: This list of bi4bi romance novels includes YA, adult romance, and a bonus polyamorous relationship novel .
item.content:encoded:
Bisexuality can get an unfairly bad rap, both from the general public and in inter-community misunderstandings. Romance novels with bisexual characters often tackle the misunderstandings and stereotypes head-on, and writers have made great strides in destigmatizing what it means to be bisexual and embracing all the exhilarating mess that comes with dating as a bisexual person. One of the most fun sub-categories of bisexual romance is the bi4bi romance plotline.

Anyone of any gender can be bisexual, so the named identity still has a lot of interesting, divergent experiences. When characters find out they have this trait in common, it’s both a bonding moment and a crystallization of differences. That’s a perfect setup for lovers to come together.

If you got through fellow contributor Rachel Brittain’s list last year, here are a bunch of fresh titles to fall in love with. This pile of bisexual reads for your TBR includes YA, adult romance, and a bonus polyamorous relationship novel to expand horizons even further.

Young Adult Bi4Bi Romance Novels

Solo Stan by Talia Tucker

Kai and Elias are both huge fans of the band CYPHR, and end up going solo and sitting next to each other. Both are on the cusp of major changes: Kai is going to college, and Elias is living in Raleigh after spending his whole life in New York City. Because of a blackout, the two boys end up in a Before Sunrise-esque, all-night adventure.

Leah on the Offbeat by Becky Albertalli

Leah was my favorite character in Simon vs. The Homo Sapiens Agenda, so I was thrilled to read the story of her coming into her own. She’s bisexual, but mostly focused on becoming a better musician and holding onto her friendships before she goes to college. She’s always had an antagonistic thing going with Abby, but there’s more going on than either of them could have anticipated. It’s a funny, sweet story about finding your sexuality as a teenager.

Adult Contemporary Bi4Bi Romance

The Pairing by Casey McQuiston

I recommend this book constantly, and I will never stop. Exes Kit and Theo are forcibly reunited on a food and wine tour of Europe, and they agree to put aside the hurt from their breakup, be friends, and compete to see who can have sex with more hot Europeans. The pursuit of pleasure is not only in sex, and part of Kit and Theo’s reunion is over their shared love of flavor. Kit flexes his pastry skills while Theo shows off an encyclopedic knowledge of wine tasting notes. Feelings, obviously, re-emerge. Side note: McQuiston has posted on Instagram that they imagined Emma D’Arcy as Theo. Maybe they can act in a quick film before the next season of House of the Dragon?

The Stand-Up Groomsman by Jackie Lau

Members of the wedding party falling in love at the wedding is a classic setup, and even better when they kind of hate each other. Vivian Liao is thrilled to be her roommate’s maid of honor, but deeply annoyed to have to deal with the groom’s best friend, Melvin Lee. Even though Melvin being an out Asian stand-up comedian helped Vivian’s own journey to becoming bi, she’s disappointed with the direction of his career. But they’re continuously thrown together, and find a lot to like about each other.

The Fiancée Farce by Alexandria Bellefleur

In a sort of Pygmalion-esque tale, Tansy Adams imagines the perfect woman (based on a book cover model) and finds Gemma, who looks like exactly what she imagined. In a convenient twist of fate, Gemma needs to get married, and she decides Tansy is the perfect companion. The marriage-of-convenience setup leads both women to fall hard for each other, and figure out if they can make the imagined relationship into something real.

Isn’t It Obvious? by Rachel Runya Katz

If you’re looking for another excellent podcast-based story with a You’ve Got Mail-inspired plot, this book is perfect. Yael has a podcast that she hosts as a secret persona called Elle, and she hires a remote editor to help her out. The editor goes by Kevin, but his name is Ravi, and Yael hates him. But as they connect over email, they meet in real life. They’re falling for each other, both in person and in the digital world.

Two’s Better by Viano Oniomoh

This friends-to-lovers story delivers high spice and a hilarious friend group. At the end of their time in university, Uzezi and Ofure haven’t had sex. So she decides they should lend each other a helping hand. They commit to keeping their friendship first, but feelings start to arise the more often they fall into bed together.

Historical Bi4Bi Romance

A Delicate Deception by Cat Sebastian

Sick of the vagaries of the social life of London, Amelia relocates to Derbyshire and commits to a life of quiet and meandering walks. Sydney, a civil engineer from the area, interrupts her solitude. Sydney and Amelia are both living on the outside of society’s expectations. Despite their growing connection, land ownership and past grievances threaten to tear them apart.

Trouble by Lex Croucher

I was surprised and delighted by this Regency-era story of a governess and a widower from Lex Croucher, both because I love The Sound of Music and because both main characters were bisexual. Emily Laurence arrives at Captain Edwards’ house assuming the role her sweet-tempered sister was supposed to take. Even though Emily is hardened, she bonds with the children and starts to connect with the captain. Like all of Croucher’s books, queerness, class, and gender roles come into play as part of the happy ending.

A Bonus Polyamorous Romance

The Threefold Tie by Aster Glenn Gray

If you are interested in exploring bisexuality in fiction past the pairing, this is a great polyamorous romance novella to start with. Jack and Everett were comrades-in-arms in the Civil War, and closer than average soldiers. After the war, Everett moves to New York and marries Sophie, whom he does love, even as he holds a candle for Jack. When Jack reappears in their lives, both Everett and Sophie are attracted to him. The struggle is finding a way to be together with all the possible struggles that will entail.

To keep the party going, you can also look for more books with bisexual characters, bisexual comics, and the most influential queer books of all time.

item.title: SUNRISE ON THE REAPING and How I’ve Changed (Some More)
item.dc:creator: Megan Mabee
item.description: I said I wouldn't read another Hunger Games novel, but SUNRISE ON THE REAPING changed my mind.
item.content:encoded:
Fifteen years ago, I read The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins in preparation for the release of the first movie. I was 18 years old, just a couple years older than Katniss’s character. Of course, I fell in love with the trilogy, devouring the next two books and seeing every movie in theaters. Nine years later, Suzanne Collins gifted the world another Hunger Games book with the release of her prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. She offered a window into the 10th annual Hunger Games through the eyes of President Snow as a young man. After reading it, I wrote an essay about how the Hunger Games prequel helped me realize I’ve changed. Flash forward five years, and she’s published another Hunger Games prequel called Sunrise on the Reaping. This one draws us into the 50th Hunger Games, back when Katniss’s mentor Haymitch gets chosen as a teen tribute.

Reading The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes in 2020 triggered quite a bit of self-reflection for me. The tragedy of the Hunger Games and the violence against children affected me more viscerally as an adult and as a mother than it did when I was a teen reader. This helped me feel more deeply the ways in which I had changed as a person. I went as far as to say that I would probably not reread the series again.

And yet, with the publication of the new Hunger Games prequel last year, I couldn’t help but feel intrigued. As I began to hear more of my friends talk about loving Haymitch’s tale, I felt my old interest perk up. The teenage me that still lingers in the fibers of my being began to tug at my peripheral. Haymitch is a more admirable character than Snow after all, and a prequel exploring his time in the Hunger Games before becoming a mentor sounded like a solid premise.

My tipping point happened this summer. I work at a library, and when one of my library patrons checked out Sunrise on the Reaping, I asked him to let me know what he thought. With the film adaptation on the horizon this November, it has been on my mind more as of late. A few weeks later, the patron returned, raving about how much he loved it. He said it was his favorite of all of them. His enthusiasm was the flint striker I needed to revisit the world of the Hunger Games.

I checked out a library copy and submerged myself within its pages. Before long, I began to feel that mesmerizing tug, that elusive feeling when a story catches you and yanks you in, like my pockets and sleeves on every drawer in my kitchen. I found myself falling in love with another Hunger Games book.

So What Makes the Sunrise on the Reaping Stand Out?

Suzanne Collins has achieved something that’s hard for many authors to do. She’s written a prequel that reads just as good, if not better, than her original popular trilogy. She did an exceptional job of tying together Sunrise on the Reaping with the characters and plots of Snow’s prequel and Katniss’s story. She threaded in new lore about the mysterious Lucy Gray Baird from Ballads, along with interesting development of characters from the original trilogy like Effie Trinket, Plutarch, Beetee, Wiress, and Mags. I find myself wanting to return to the original trilogy and reread it, something I once thought I wouldn’t do again.

Collins layered more depth into this prequel as well. Her literary allusions shine and become more apparent in Sunrise. Like Lucy Gray Baird’s connections to Wordsworth’s Lucy Gray in Songbirds, Collins connects Lenore Dove from Sunrise to Edgar Allan Poe’s The Raven.

Her allusions go beyond poetry, though. She also continues to bring to mind classics in dystopian literature. Just as the Hunger Games nods to Shirley Jackson’s The Lottery, and Peeta’s traumatic conditioning in Mockingjay calls back to Burgess’s Clockwork Orange, the piercing tone installed in Lou Lou’s ear feels reminiscent of Vonnegut’s “Harrison Bergeron.” Collins has interwoven these allusions into her stories in ways that are emotional and thought-provoking.

Through Haymitch’s story, Collins also digs into grief, loss, purpose, and hope in ways that feel deeper and more nuanced than her previous works. Perhaps, it comes with her recognizing that the teens who fell in love with her books all those years ago have grown up now.

What’s Different About Me Now as a Reader?

When I was a teen, I read for entertainment. I read to lose myself in a book, to feel an imaginary world enclose around me every time I opened it. When I was in my 20s, I read for much the same reasons, though I started to expand my literary horizons, especially as I began working in libraries.

However, when I wrote my essay on The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes in 2020, I was a 27-year-old mother to a two-year-old son. The two of us were living on our own together at the beginning of COVID. It was a hard time in my life. As the world shifted outside with the fear and isolation of the early COVID years, my internal world shifted as I adjusted to life as a new mother. Reading the tragedy within Songbirds at this time devastated me. While I enjoyed the story overall, especially Lucy Gray’s whimsical character, I couldn’t get past the darkness of the Hunger Games.

It’s been six years, nearly to the day, that I read that prequel and wrote that essay. Now, I’m a 33-year-old mother to an almost eight-year-old son. I’ve weathered more in life since I last fell under the Hunger Games’ spell, and I’ve continued to grow as a reader. While reading for entertainment and escape is still important to me, I also read to think and to feel something. I read books that help me understand other people’s perspectives, as well as stories that feel relatable to my own experiences. Through reading, I hope to see other people more clearly. I hope to feel more seen, too.

As I read Sunrise on the Reaping, I drew more meaning from it than I did Songbirds and Snakes. After much devastation in Sunrise, Plutarch reassures Haymitch, “You were capable of imagining a different future. And maybe it won’t be realized today, maybe not in our lifetime. Maybe it will take generations. We’re all part of a continuum. Does that make it pointless?”

These are the kinds of words I’ll carry with me. When I’m feeling the hardness of life, like I once did during those lonely COVID years, I’ll return to these words. That’s the kind of impact I’m seeking when I read a book now.

A Last Thought…

Reading Sunrise on the Reaping made me think and feel, and it enveloped me in a comforting nostalgia that I hadn’t tasted in a long time. While the story had many dark moments, Haymitch’s perseverance amidst it all reminded me of Katniss’s journey and how I felt reading about her as a teen, devouring the original trilogy with a ferocity I often miss now.

While the days as a teen where I could spend hours reading without a care in the world have passed, I felt an inkling of that spark again while reading this Hunger Games prequel. Despite all of the ways I’ve changed, I’m also still a girl who will read a book in a coffee shop and start crying as I reach the last page. I’m still a girl who spills tea on her library books and rambles about the stories she loves. We can grow as readers, and we can find ourselves again in the books we read.

Our feelings about fandoms like the Hunger Games may wax and wane like the phases of the moon. Yet as I read each Hunger Games book, I feel connected to something bigger than me. Suzanne Collins’s books have touched the lives of so many people, and I’m glad to be a part of that. For as Haymitch reflects upon one of Lenore Dove’s sentiments in Sunrise, “Each book’s as precious as a person, she says, as it preserves someone’s thoughts and feelings long after they’re gone.”

item.title: New Picture Books Featuring Grandparents in Honor of Grandparents Day
item.dc:creator: Alison Doherty
item.description: These five beautiful picture books about grandparents celebrate the amazing role grandparents play in children's lives.
item.content:encoded:
In the United States, it is Grandparents Day this weekend. The relationship between grandparents and grandchildren is so special and definitely something to celebrate! I got to experience the magic of it with my grandparents when I was growing up, with summer visits, special celebrations, and a big chunk of time where one set of my grandparents lived just one block away. And now that I have a two-year-old, I’ve gotten to see up close the beautiful relationship between my son and my parents develop right from the beginning. My son loves it whenever he gets to see his grandparents, whether that’s in person or on a video call, and he adores fictional grandparent characters in books and other media (we may or may not have watched the “Visiting Grandpere” episode of Daniel Tiger over ten times at this point).

I know my son isn’t alone because when I started looking for picture books to celebrate Grandparents Day this year, I found almost 20 picture books featuring grandparents published in the last year alone. And there were probably even more! I thought it was so beautiful to read about how grandparents care for their grandchildren, offer them deep understanding, and pass down culture and family traditions. From a grandson’s invitation to slow down and spend time together when visiting Granddad to a Bubbe and Granddaughter making a summer bucket list, these five beautiful stories celebrate the amazing role grandparents play in children’s lives.

5 New Picture Books Featuring Grandparents

Spendin’ Time by Gary R. Gray Jr., illustrated by Rahele Jomepour Bell

On a trip to visit his grandparents, a young boy and his Granddad leave the house with a list from his Nan of food to pick up for her to make dinner. But instead of completing the errand with maximum efficiency, as the boy expects, Granddad suggests going berry picking, and even sneaking in ice cream before dinner. And while they are “spendin’ time” together, Grandad points out the important places and memories in their Nova Scotia town. The sweetness continues when the duo is greeted by Nan’s delicious apple pie. Nobody will spoil you like your grandparents! And this book celebrates that special relationship and the connections older generations give young people to the past.

The Explorers by Dee Hahn, illustrated by Ashlyn Anstee

Etta and Grandma Maisie have been going on adventures together for years. Etta’s mom and dad think their love of earthworm castles, gnome mazes, and bizarre food combinations is a bit odd, but Etta and Grandma Maisie have always understood each other. This year, they are both facing big changes: Etta is going to kindergarten, and Grandma Maisie is moving into a retirement home. At first, both of them feel misunderstood and weird, and it makes them each avoid meeting new people. But both learn to let their guard down when they find a pair of kindred spirits at the Grandparents’ Picnic. And they decide that they can still keep some things special to themselves, while still making new friends as well.

Where I Grew by Jashar Awan, illustrated by Rahele Jomepour Bell

A grandfather and granddaughter take a walk through the forest. As they walk, they make connections between different elements in nature and their own family’s story. The granddaughter reflects on how her family worked hard to find the perfect place to both literally and figuratively put down roots. And she thinks about how this has influenced her life and will influence the future generations of her family. With soft illustrations and beautiful, sparse text, this book is a beautiful reflection on how grandparents connect children to larger family journeys.

Becca and Bubbe’s Bucket List by Laura Gehl, illustrated by Sarah Lynn Baker

On the first day of summer, Becca learns about the concept of a bucket list from her Bubbe, who has crossed all but one item off hers. Together, they make a summer bucket list and work together to cross off Becca’s items. Having a water balloon fight is easy. And it’s delicious to order the giant ice cream sundae. But some items, like swimming in the ocean, are too hard to do without the help of Bubbe. And then at the end of summer, Becca gets the help of the other neighborhood grandmas to give Bubbe the chance to cross the last item off her bucket list.

The River of Caregiving by Jocelyn Chung, illustrated by Sarah Gonzales

This story begins with the narrator’s A-ma telling her that in their family, care flows between members like a river. This causes the child to look closer at the ways different people within their intergenerational family unit take care of each other in their daily lives. Her A-gong picks her up from school, and she translates for him when he has a doctor’s appointment. Her mother helps to bathe and dress A-ma, the way A-ma dressed her mother when she was a little girl. With extended family, there are care packages, gatherings for celebrations, and thoughtful check-ins as signs of care. This story really highlights how central the grandparents are to setting the tone of the family’s values of love, care, and reciprocity.

These five new picture books about grandparents show that no matter what you call them, the love grandparents have for their grandchildren is both special and singular. If you are celebrating Grandparents Day this weekend with any young readers, I suggest picking one or more of them up. And if you are lucky enough to have grandparents still in your life, maybe give them a call or send them a card to let them know how much they mean to you!

And for more grandparent love, here are even more children’s books about grandparents, and some of our favorite literary grandparents.

item.title: 📚 Saddle up
item.dc:creator: Community
item.description: Netflix orders Lonesome Dove series from East of Eden team.
item.content:encoded:
September 10, 2026View Online | Join All Access | Listen

Need a dose of inspiration? Allow us to point you to the new PBS documentary, Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World. You won’t find better motivation to get out there, touch some grass, and really live your one wild and precious life. More on Oliver, who would have been 91 today, below.

Spread the word. Share this email with friends.

THE HEADLINE

Netflix wrangles Lonesome Dove series

Saddle up, pals. Netflix has ordered a series adaptation of Larry McMurtry’s Lonesome Dove.

  • The beloved western doorstopper was a smash hit upon its publication in 1985 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction the following year.
  • Robert Duvall and Tommy Lee Jones starred in a popular TV miniseries adaptation for CBS in 1989.

At the helm of the new series are Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart, whose adaptation of another epic—Steinbeck’s East of Eden—lands on Netflix next month.

  • Jinny Howe, head of scripted series for the U.S. and Canada at the streamer, praised the duo: “After East of Eden, we know exactly what they’re capable of — the depth of character, the sweep of place, the emotional precision. This material deserves that level of care. In their hands, it’s going to be something extraordinary.”

Production details, including casting and release date, are TBD. We’re betting on fall 2028.

In the meantime, you can join our guided read-along of East of Eden.

BOOKSHELF TIME MACHINE

Power ranking the books of 2006

Twitter was brand new. Wii Sports took over your living room. “SexyBack” was on the radio—we still listened to the radio—and The Devil Wears Prada ruled the box office.

The year was 2006, and the books were, well, the books were as they always are: all over the place.

  • Eat, Pray, Love gave white ladies everywhere a new way to explain their divorces, and The Secret promised a new way to happiness.
  • The Road ran the awards circuit alongside The Inheritance of Loss, which claimed trophies and hearts.
  • Indie booksellers propelled Water for Elephants to word-of-mouth bestsellerdom.
  • The Audacity of Hope announced the arrival of a serious presidential contender and a new view on the American Dream.

Listen as we power rank these and more of the books of 2006 on the Book Riot Podcast.

RESISTING THE FEED

Celebrating 25 years of Feed by M.T. Anderson

The iconic YA dystopian novel Feed by M. T. Anderson will turn 25 years old next year, and today, Book Riot is revealing the new cover!

Check out the high-resolution version, plus some behind-the-scenes insight into its design, in the What’s Up in YA newsletter.

We also interviewed M. T. Anderson about the impact of his novel 25 years later. Here’s an excerpt:

Feed is dedicated to “All those who resist the feed.” What does resisting the feed look like in 2026?

It’s harder now than it was then! So much of the way we live our lives and conduct business has been subsumed by the algorithms. Seriously, the other day I was trying to buy some bed pillows, and I was exhausted by looking online for something that you really need to handle to judge appropriately, and I thought to myself, I wish there was just like some PLACE where you could go and there’d be a bunch of pillows and you could compare them. For a millisecond, I literally found myself reinventing the store. (One old-fashioned note in Feed, by the way, is that you can detect that I myself am not fully able to shake the centrality of the mall as the place we go to buy. Now, of course, I’m nostalgic for malls!)

Resisting the feed means being aware of all the choices we’re actually making, even the ones we’re not invited to recognize. At this point, for example, we should all be aware of the way that the cognitive off-loading onto AI has a very real neurological cost. Without literally inserting any feed-like device into the wetware, we’re in danger of rewiring ourselves even further for corporate subservience and the kind of blindness that comes of accepting a corporatized reality. Considering the other dire issues that face our world at the moment, that blindness will be absolutely disastrous. AI, as in Feed, is always willing to whisper to us, “All shall be well. All manner of things shall be well.”

Read the full interview at Book Riot.

TRENDS

Nonfiction isn’t selling like it used to.

This observation from Sean Delone’s recent post in his newsletter called Dear Head of Mine caught my eye:

“What has happened in the last ten years is that the overall industry has grown modestly, but fiction and nonfiction have basically flipped positions. In 2015, 6 of the top 25 bestselling hardcover books—this is a not-perfect but useful proxy for new books published—were fiction. In 2025, 18 of the top 25 hardcover books were fiction, meaning only 7 were nonfiction, almost an exact inversion of ten years ago.”

Broader industry data is perhaps more conclusive: over the last four years, adult fiction sales are up 30%, whereas adult nonfiction sales are basically flat.

  • Denone thinks this a gender story, which would generally comport with historical splits between men and women when it comes to non-fiction consumption.

My first thought was podcasts, which several of the commenters suggested as well. But then I remembered this post by Tim Ferriss (The 4-Hour Workweek), which has has been rattling around in my brain. Ferriss has seen sales of his portfolio of nonfiction tiles, which he called a kind-of annuity for its regularity, drop 80% since 2022. His culprit seems much clearer and more ominous:

“ChatGPT, powered by the updated GPT-3.5 model, launched on November 30, 2022.”

And my guess is that these forces are all at work. Men are reading less, people are listening to more podcasts for their non-fiction adjacent content, and they are using LLMs to get longer-form, Google-on-steroids information. Cannot say I love this. — JO

AUDIOBOOKS

The latest and greatest at Audible

What’s next in your listening queue? Need a little help deciding? Here are three new audiobooks available for Audible members, including an Audible exclusive.

  • The Disappearers by Marlon James, read by a full cast: James’ highly-anticipated novel about the murder of a gay man in 1980s Jamaica and its tragic, far-reaching consequences is being lauded as a modern masterpiece. It has already been longlisted for the Booker Prize.
  • Tell the Ghosts I’m Gone by Kalynn Bayron, read by Jordan Cobb: A horror novel about a group of teens who each possess special gifts, where “special” just might mean deadly. We get queer found family, ghost-hunting, spiritualist lore, and a supernatural mystery, too.
  • The Murder at the Vicarage by Agatha Christie, read by a full cast: The Christie classic that introduced the world to the iconic Miss Marple is worth revisiting for this fact alone: this new Audible Exclusive version features full-cast narration led by an icon in her own right: Toni Collette. —VD
POP CULTURE

Heated Rivalry and queer hockey culture

Daniel Gawthrop is the author of Cutting Edge: Hockey as Queer Culture, out this week from Arsenal Pulp Press. Below, he describes responses to the Heated Rivalry TV series in the LGBTQ+ community. (Spoilers ahead!)

After season 1 of Heated Rivalry began streaming late last year, queer community response to the series ranged from unqualified raves to critiques about sex scene authenticity and obsession with the sexual identity of its two principal actors. For many of us, Heated Rivalry was a breath of fresh air from a mainstream TV world hardly abundant with stories of queer happiness—never mind gay male athletes in hypermasculine sports who are unafraid of being vulnerable with each other.

Season 1’s episode 5, where Scott Hunter calls his lover Kip down from the stands to the ice after he’s won “the Cup” to kiss him on live television, was huge. Outsports reported that viewing parties for that episode led to groups of gay men buying tickets to their first NHL games and others watching TV hockey despite knowing little about the sport. For the Cutting Edges, Vancouver’s LBGTQ+ hockey association, there was a massive surge of interest from queer folk wanting to return to hockey or play it for the first time.

Some even used Heated Rivalry to come out. 40-year-old Minnesota native Jesse Kortuem, who left the sport at 17 and later played competitively from the closet, had returned to hockey by playing in queer tournaments as a guest of the Cutting Edges and other teams. A Facebook post citing the Edges’ warm welcome and Heated Rivalry as factors in his decision to come out went viral, landing Kortuem an appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show. His host surprised him with a video greeting of congrats by Hudson Williams, who plays Shane Hollander. (Williams later reported that real-life closeted pro athletes, including hockey players, had reached out to him for inspiration.)

For others, Heated Rivalry was triggering. Former Ontario Hockey League and minor pro goaltender Brock McGillis—now in high demand on the speaking circuit—had a panic attack while watching the first half of episode 1, which reminded him of the years he’d spent fearful of exposure. He came to enjoy the series, but said it wouldn’t convince closeted NHL players to come out. So far, he’s right.

HAPPY BIRTHDAY

Mary Oliver, born September 10, 1935

Did you know? As a teenager, Oliver became friends with Edna St. Vincent Millay’s sister, Norma, and spent several years helping her go through her sister’s papers.

CRITICAL LINKING

You are now free to roam about the internet

The cast of the the upcoming Bell Jar adaptation is stacked.

Let’s talk about what you’re reading in September.

Authors are getting their settlements from the landmark Anthropic AI lawsuit, and it’s not going great.

Sure, here’s a list of books for lingerie lovers.

item.title: One of The Best YA Books of the Century Turns 25: On M.T. Anderson’s FEED
item.dc:creator: Kelly Jensen
item.description: M.T. Anderson's FEED, one of the best YA books of the century, turns 25 next year. It's getting a new cover, too.
item.content:encoded:
“We went to the moon to have fun, but the moon turned out to completely suck.”

One of the most iconic opening lines in young adult fiction is also a line that helped launch a century full of outstanding, boundary-pushing, prescient, and memorable books for teen readers. Written by M.T. Anderson, Feed is a work of dystopia about Titus and his friends having their spring break plans completely upended when the feeds inside them malfunction. What follows is a story about a girl who has always lived beyond the tech-designated range of human feelings, helping Titus, his friends, and the greater world find meaning and purpose after the hijacking.

Published in 2002, Feed was light-years ahead of its time in thinking about the role of technology in our world. The story resonates deeply today, with many of the very predictions made 25 years ago now real issues being grappled with. Themes of consumerism and algorithms as identity collide with deeply human experiences of first love, friendship, and adventure.

I first picked up Feed when I began my career as a teen librarian. I’d spent a day doing professional development on audiobooks, led by librarians who’d been leaders in reviewing, promoting, and awarding the best of the best in audio production. They urged those of us who hadn’t yet read Anderson’s novel in print to pick it up on audio, and those who’d only read it in print to go back and listen to it. Feed remains one of my gold standards not only for YA dystopia but also for excellence in audiobook production and performance. Listening to this with headphones is an especially trippy and memorable experience.

The book has stuck with me for the years since, and it’s one I could not be more excited to have nominated as one of the Best YA Books of the Century (So Far). It’s been wildly influential to YA as a whole, including to many beloved authors who’ve called Anderson’s book a masterclass in writing for teen readers. Years after first experiencing Feed, I coordinated a multi-library event with young adult writer Siobhan Vivian for teens. Anderson’s opening line was one she referenced when leading a teen writing workshop as part of the event–and she’s far from the only author who points to Feed as an example of getting it right.

In 2027, Feed will celebrate its 25th anniversary. Readers will be able to pick up a dazzling new edition of the classic next spring, featuring a brand new cover. I’m thrilled to share that cover exclusively.

But before doing that, a moment for the iconic 2001 design:

The cover features the back of Gregg Hammerquist’s head. Hammerquist has been working at Candlewick–Feed‘s publisher–since 2001, where he’s now the Senior Director of Group Graphic Production.

“Prior to the design featuring my head, there was an approved cover design which featured a group of young people,” said Hammerquist, “Literally, days before we needed to get files to the printer, there was a decision made to try a different direction. The designer grabbed our office camera (this was years before iPhones were a thing) and asked me to go to the wall and turn around. She snapped the shot, did some color adjusting, and crossed her fingers.”

Covers at the time were discussed in weekly meetings, and Hammerquist noted that their office was open concept. He overheard the conversation about his head taking center stage.

“When the designer (Caroline Lawrence) presented her comp which featured my head to the group, the Head of Editorial at the time (Liz Bicknell) said “I think we should make his neck thinner”. I immediately thought to myself “Good Grief!,” he said. “As someone who loves going to the gym and being strong, the last thing I wanted was parts of me to be made smaller/thinner.”

The good news is that the design team elected to keep his neck exactly as-is when the book went to press.

So what does the cover celebrating the 25th anniversary of a beloved story and a memorable cover look like? Is the head still there?

Wait no longer. Here it is:

You’ll immediately notice that the new look takes everything that made the original and cranks it up a few notches. While the title now takes up much more real estate, it doesn’t erase what made Feed‘s cover Feed‘s cover.

“We wanted our cover to be a proper celebration of the story’s enduring legacy,” explained Larsson McSwain, Assistant Art Director at Candlewick. “This is a redesign for M. T. Anderson’s long-time fans and new readers alike.”

The new cover plays into many of the trends we see in cover design right now–printed edges worthy of display on shelves and on social media posts. While it retains Hammerquist’s head, it tweaks the text running across the entire background. Where the 2001 edition uses words to show off the feed, the new edition turns to binary. It’s a smart choice. The binary numbers don’t detract from the bold title font and styling.

“Retaining the head was a no-brainer; but we revamped the color palette (electric!), updated the type design (bold!), and adorned the book with eye-catching effects,” said McSwain. McSwain emphasized that the design team knew that they “had to keep the head.”

For new and established fans of the book, using its first line is the perfect choice for the four-color printed edges.

The 25th-anniversary edition of Feed will hit shelves on May 11, 2027, but you can preorder it now. If this is a book you haven’t read, it’s one to make sure is on your TBR; if it’s a book with which you have familiarity, consider a reread–it not only holds up, but it remains an example of the variety of teen characters that exist in YA to entertain and challenge readers, young and not-so-young.

Want more? You’re in luck. Read this fantastic new interview with M.T. Anderson about Feed, its enduring legacy, and its 25th anniversary.

item.title: Heated Rivalry and Queer Hockey Culture
item.dc:creator: Community
item.description: Daniel Gawthrop, author of Cutting Edge: Hockey as Queer Culture describes responses to the Heated Rivalry TV series in the LGBTQ+ community.
item.content:encoded:
Daniel Gawthrop is the author of Cutting Edge: Hockey as Queer Culture, out this week from Arsenal Pulp Press. Below, he describes responses to the Heated Rivalry TV series in the LGBTQ+ community. (Spoilers ahead!)

After season 1 of Heated Rivalry began streaming late last year, queer community response to the series ranged from unqualified raves to critiques about sex scene authenticity and obsession with the sexual identity of its two principal actors. For many of us, Heated Rivalry was a breath of fresh air from a mainstream TV world hardly abundant with stories of queer happiness—never mind gay male athletes in hypermasculine sports who are unafraid of being vulnerable with each other.

Season 1’s episode 5, where Scott Hunter calls his lover Kip down from the stands to the ice after he’s won “the Cup” to kiss him on live television, was huge. Outsports reported that viewing parties for that episode led to groups of gay men buying tickets to their first NHL games and others watching TV hockey despite knowing little about the sport. For the Cutting Edges, Vancouver’s LBGTQ+ hockey association, there was a massive surge of interest from queer folk wanting to return to hockey or play it for the first time.

Some even used Heated Rivalry to come out. 40-year-old Minnesota native Jesse Kortuem, who left the sport at 17 and later played competitively from the closet, had returned to hockey by playing in queer tournaments as a guest of the Cutting Edges and other teams. A Facebook post citing the Edges’ warm welcome and Heated Rivalry as factors in his decision to come out went viral, landing Kortuem an appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show. His host surprised him with a video greeting of congrats by Hudson Williams, who plays Shane Hollander. (Williams later reported that real-life closeted pro athletes, including hockey players, had reached out to him for inspiration.)

For others, Heated Rivalry was triggering. Former Ontario Hockey League and minor pro goaltender Brock McGillis—now in high demand on the speaking circuit—had a panic attack while watching the first half of episode 1, which reminded him of the years he’d spent fearful of exposure. He came to enjoy the series, but said it wouldn’t convince closeted NHL players to come out. So far, he’s right.

item.title: Celebrating 25 Years of FEED by M.T. Anderson
item.dc:creator: Danika Ellis
item.description: We interviewed M. T. Anderson about his iconic YA dystopian novel, Feed, turning 25 next year. Plus, a cover reveal for the new edition!
item.content:encoded:
In 2027, the iconic YA dystopian novel Feed by M. T. Anderson will turn 25 years old, and today, Book Riot is revealing the new cover!

Check out the high-resolution version, plus some behind-the-scenes insight into its design, in the What’s Up in YA newsletter.

We also interviewed M. T. Anderson about the impact of his novel 25 years later. Here’s what he had to say.

In earlier editions of Feed, you discuss the events of the novel as allegorical and satirical—not as predictions. But 25 years later, the feed feels closer to reality than ever, between social media feeds, AI, and technology like smart glasses. How has your perception of the feed of the novel changed since it was first published?

When I wrote Feed, back in 2001, I really didn’t take the tech literally. The feed directly implanted in the brain was just supposed to evoke what was already true and what had been true even when I was a teen: the voice of advertising was in our heads, making demands, distorting our sense of possibility and our view of who we wanted to be. I felt it was obliterating our sense of self, our eccentricities, and perhaps most importantly, our understanding of how the world we relied on actually worked.

Of course, in many ways, the speed of tech development and the reluctance to intelligently regulate it have made all those problems even worse. We rely more deeply on systems of incredible complexity that are beyond our control. But also, our relationship to consumerism has changed in an era of consolidated corporate power and stunning wealth inequality, and that wasn’t something I fully predicted in Feed.

Feed was about a world where we’re being sold things all the time; but now it feels like we live in a world where we’re the ones having to sell ourselves, market ourselves, all the time. Social media, the attention economy—which was only an idea when I wrote Feed—started that trend, but the costs of home and health care and even just food have made us all aware of the fragility of our economic lives in a world where money always seems to drift upwards, out of our grasp. The false sense of security in Feed has given way to a generalized anxiety.

In 2017, I wrote a kind of follow-up to Feed—not in the same world at all, but an updated vision of this situation where we’re all intent on selling ourselves, called Landscape with Invisible Hand, about a kid who wants to be a landscape painter doing Hudson River School paintings after an alien invasion. Earth has become a sort of economic backwater in someone else’s empire. In that book, I made some predictions about the economic and social effects of advanced AI (and useless AI packages in devices that don’t need them). I never would have predicted, though, that we would really have credible AI in place as rapidly as we did. I believed I had to create aliens to introduce it.

To predict the future, you don’t need to know much about tech. You just have to know about capitalism.

Feed is dedicated to “All those who resist the feed.” What does resisting the feed look like in 2026?

It’s harder now than it was then! So much of the way we live our lives and conduct business has been subsumed by the algorithms. Seriously, the other day I was trying to buy some bed pillows, and I was exhausted by looking online for something that you really need to handle to judge appropriately, and I thought to myself, I wish there was just like some PLACE where you could go and there’d be a bunch of pillows and you could compare them. For a millisecond, I literally found myself reinventing the store. (One old-fashioned note in Feed, by the way, is that you can detect that I myself am not fully able to shake the centrality of the mall as the place we go to buy. Now, of course, I’m nostalgic for malls!)

Resisting the feed means being aware of all the choices we’re actually making, even the ones we’re not invited to recognize. At this point, for example, we should all be aware of the way that the cognitive off-loading onto AI has a very real neurological cost. Without literally inserting any feed-like device into the wetware, we’re in danger of rewiring ourselves even further for corporate subservience and the kind of blindness that comes of accepting a corporatized reality. Considering the other dire issues that face our world at the moment, that blindness will be absolutely disastrous. AI, as in Feed, is always willing to whisper to us, “All shall be well. All manner of things shall be well.”

There are references to U.S. American politics woven throughout the novel. Is Feed is an allegory specific to the United States?

It was at the time. It was begun in August 2001, just weeks before 9/11. The United States seemed unassailable, the world’s great unilateral power, for better or worse. I used to say that the world is always already dystopian: it’s just that we happen to live in the shining capital. That’s no longer so true. The lessons of the last twenty-five years have shown us our fragility. Even the white middle class in America can feel that systems are falling apart. That’s a difficult thing, but ultimately a good thing.

By the way, because the president in the book is the crapulent, foul-mouthed President Trumbull, I’ve been asked if, in 2001, I magically predicted that Trump would be elected.

No. I did not.

Though he did, a few days ago, attempt to annex the moon.

[SPOILERS FOR FEED] The relationship between Titus and Violet is very different than other YA “sicklit” novels of the 90s, or stories like A Walk to Remember. Titus is not the romantic hero we have come to expect. Was that a deliberate response to these kinds of stories?

That wasn’t really a conscious decision on my part. Just a sense that this boy, Titus, is self-involved and has been trained to focus on positive selling points. I didn’t know where the novel was going when I started writing it, and I just found him naturally behaving badly as Violet deteriorated. He doesn’t want to confront what’s going on with her. But I wonder if I would have done any better at his age. The discomfort of others’ suffering is something we often turn away from. I wanted to make him a somewhat torn character: he has sudden impulses where he’s wishing to be better, but he’s formed entirely by this stultifying world where no one is being encouraged to really think for themselves if it’s uncomfortable.

What are some of your favorite sci-fi/dystopian novels of the past 25 years?

Some old stand-bys: Shaun Tan’s picture book The Rabbits is one of the best, most chilling, and most succinct dystopian texts on imperialism that could be imagined. His wordless graphic novel The Arrival was one of the best books of the Noughts and forces the reader to experience what it’s like for a refugee from a dystopian nation to try to resettle in another, alien nation where the rules are all different. Please get this into the hands of teens as we debate asylum-seeker and refugee status in this country.

For a lusciously written, wildly colorful sci-fi romance that takes place across many war-shattered dystopian times and worlds, check out Amal El-Mohtar and Max Gladstone’s This Is How You Lose the Time War, about two military assassins who fall inconveniently in love while hunting each other.

If we can sneak one in from just before the turn of the millennium, Ben Marcus’s Age of Wire and String is a set of missives from a mind-bending, Dadaist dystopia, at once banal and yet utterly unfamiliar.

For a more realistic dystopia, Lily Brooks-Dalton, in The Light Pirate, has written a convincing and sobering portrait of how climate collapse could play out in a small Florida town.

And finally, if you want a truly dismal dystopian reading experience, just read any high-school-level world history textbook from cover to cover in one sitting. We have got to be better. I believe we can be.

item.title: The Trailer for the New CARRIE Adaptation Is Out
item.dc:creator: Community
item.description: The latest CARRIE adaptation—led by Mike Flanagan—feels fresh, but diverges a bit from the original story.
item.content:encoded:
The official trailer for the latest adaptation of Carrie by Stephen King is out.

It starts off with an introduction to Carrie White as she goes through her high school’s metal detectors. As the socially awkward, previously homeschooled girl becomes more accustomed to public schooling, the tension ratchets up.

Soon, we see Carrie’s eagerness for school clash with her classmates’ cruelty, all while a narrator hints at a fateful, unexplainable and violent day.

Many of us know King’s Carrie and know what to expect, but this adaptation feels of our time—in a good way. The modern additions—like Carrie’s bullying happening over the internet for all to watch on their smartphones—make sense and help to bring the character’s issues into the modern day.

For more on how the series differs from the book and what to expect, check out our rundown.

The Mike Flanagan-led series stars Summer H. Howell, Matthew Lillard, Amber Midthunder, and others. It will run for eight episodes (so far) on Prime Video, starting on October 7.
